title: A focused HTTP workbench for power users
question: Choose the visual direction. Every option keeps familiar collections, request tabs, an editor, and response inspection; these are visual systems, not unusual controls.

options.label: Chromatic notation
options.thesis: Make the provenance of every reused value legible without leaving the request.
options.viewport: Collections left; environment and request tabs above; URL and Send over a request/response split; a selected response value reveals a compact source-to-use inspector.
options.risk: Semantic colors must stay sparse and labeled or dense data becomes visually noisy.

raised.raise: Use exact tabular alignment and stable widths throughout execution metadata.
Use plain-language empty states and comfortably sized primary controls.
Maintain stable request context while inspecting deeply nested response fields.
Give each request a consistent identity across collections, tabs, and history without mascots.
Always expose the next recovery action when a variable or execution fails.

options.label: Engineering reference
options.lineage: Well-edited engineering documentation and cross-reference indexes
options.thesis: An exceptionally readable workbench where every value can lead back to its source.
options.viewport: Collections left, request editor center, response inspector right; source links open an inline provenance note without replacing the response.
options.risk: Familiar and effective, but closest to where polished developer tools already land.

options.label: Execution board
options.lineage: Live departure boards and segmented travel documents
options.thesis: Make the latest execution and every changed result impossible to misread.
options.viewport: Standard collection sidebar and request/response panes, with a compact execution history whose changed fields stay marked until acknowledged.
options.case: Matches product clarity through persistent change tracking, but has weaker identification with code-centric power users.
options.risk: Execution history could compete with the editor if given too much space.

options.label: Data-sublime field
options.thesis: A strictly black-and-white HTTP workbench at maximum numeric density.
options.viewport: Familiar request and response panes with precise numeric execution columns; selected fields isolate related values.
options.case: Loses audience identification and product clarity: extreme contrast and density weaken long-session scanning.
options.kept: Exact tabular alignment, not barcode ornament or strobing.
options.risk: No color channel for errors, methods, or dependency roles.

options.label: Warm consumer surface
options.thesis: A friendly HTTP workbench with soft surfaces and plain-language feedback.
options.viewport: Standard editor panes use comfortable spacing and a single saturated action color; inline feedback explains failures.
options.case: Loses audience identification and product clarity at power-user density: generous cards consume working space.
options.kept: Clear language and comfortably sized primary actions.
options.risk: Could feel introductory rather than expert.

options.label: Lexicon shoulder
options.thesis: Treat nested response inspection as precise reference reading.
options.viewport: Familiar request and response panes retain response ancestry beside the selected field; technical data stays monospace.
options.case: Loses audience identification and product clarity: long-form typographic grammar is less suitable for editable dense HTTP data.
options.kept: Stable context while inspecting deeply nested fields.
options.risk: Book-like text treatment can overpower the workbench.

options.label: Character catalog
options.thesis: Give saved requests a strong, consistent identity across the workspace.
options.viewport: Standard collections and editor panes repeat a request’s identity in its tab and history entry; no mascot or ranked request grid.
options.case: Loses audience identification and product clarity: playful differentiation competes with method and status semantics.
options.kept: Stable identity across collection, tab, and history.
options.risk: Unrelated color identities could fight syntax highlighting.

options.label: Airport wayfinding
options.thesis: Expose the next useful action when an HTTP workflow breaks.
options.viewport: Standard collection sidebar and request/response split; unresolved values expose one clear source link and recovery action.
options.case: Loses audience identification and product clarity: navigation emphasis competes with the request and response payloads.
options.kept: Explicit next recovery action, not airport signs or arrows.
options.risk: Large yellow regions can dominate a long editing session.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: A familiar API client, executed with exceptional precision.
canonCard.viewport: Collection tree, URL bar, editor tabs, response pane, and collapsible history.
canonCard.risk: Intentionally less visually differentiated from existing API clients.
